title: Competition
objective: After this level you can explain how competition pushes prices down and quality up.
summary: In perfect competition, each seller is a price taker. Profits attract new rivals, which pushes prices down. Competition keeps prices down and quality up.

cards.headline: Try selling your corn above the market price. Watch what happens.
cards.body: Nothing happens. That's the problem: no buyers come at all. Meet the quiet force that works for you every time you shop.

cards.headline: Price takers
cards.body: In perfect competition, many firms sell identical products to many buyers, everyone knows the prices, and firms can come and go freely. A single corn farmer can't pick her price: supply and demand across the whole market set it. Ask more and buyers get the same corn from somebody else. Economists call her a price taker. The market names the price; she just takes it.

cards.headline: Profits attract rivals
cards.body: So what stops a whole industry charging a fortune? Newcomers. When sellers in a competitive market earn fat profits, new firms pile in. Their extra supply brings the price down, until the extra profit is squeezed away and nobody else wants to join. High profits are an open invitation.

cards.fact: Competition keeps prices down and quality up.
cards.context: That's how the US Federal Trade Commission puts it. When businesses must compete for your money, they have strong incentives to run efficiently, keep prices down and keep quality up. For shoppers, that adds up to lower prices, better products and services, more choice and more new ideas.

cards.headline: Competition: understood
learned: Competition keeps prices down and quality up

questions.prompt: In perfect competition, what is a price taker?

options.label: A firm that must accept the market price
A buyer who always pays the asking price
options.rationale: The term describes sellers in a competitive market.

options.label: A government that sets prices
options.rationale: In perfect competition, nobody sets the price.

options.label: A firm that sets whatever price it likes

questions.explanation: With many sellers of identical products, one firm has to accept the price the whole market sets.

questions.prompt: Sellers in a competitive market are earning big profits. What does competition predict?

options.label: Prices rise even higher
options.rationale: Entry adds supply, which pulls prices down.

options.label: The government fixes the price
options.rationale: No law is needed; newcomers do the work.

options.label: New firms enter and the price falls
The existing sellers merge into one
options.rationale: Profits attract rivals; they don't create mergers.

questions.explanation: Profits attract new firms. Their extra supply brings the price down until the extra profit is gone.

questions.prompt: Why does a corn farmer who asks more than Level 44's equilibrium price find no buyers?

options.label: Buyers can get the same corn from many other sellers
The law forbids selling above equilibrium
options.rationale: No law is needed; competition does it.

options.label: Buyers only want corn when prices are rising
options.rationale: Buyers want less at higher prices, not more.

questions.explanation: With many sellers of identical corn at the market price, nobody pays extra to one farmer.
